claims.text: The initial relatively high-Ta TiZrHfTax alloy is predominantly single-phase BCC.
Reducing Ta content destabilizes the BCC phase and causes an HCP phase to appear within the BCC matrix.
The HCP phase can be produced as finely dispersed precipitates.
The HCP precipitates are elastically nearly isotropic.
Vacuum melting followed by solution treatment and aging at 700–900 °C will promote controlled HCP precipitation in a BCC matrix.
The proposed processing can produce a fine, evenly distributed HCP precipitate network that remains effective at room and moderately elevated temperatures.
Decreasing Ta softens the BCC matrix and thereby promotes ductile behavior.
The HCP precipitates have enhanced resistance to shear and therefore strengthen the dual-phase alloy.
HCP precipitates strengthen the alloy by obstructing dislocation motion.
HCP precipitates improve fracture resistance by blunting or deflecting propagating cracks.
Combining a softened BCC matrix with shear-resistant HCP precipitates can improve the strength–ductility combination.
The dual-phase microstructure will optimize or beneficially balance Young's modulus.
The modified alloy will have a yield strength greater than 800 MPa.
The modified alloy will have tensile ductility of at least 12%.
The modified alloy will have greater fracture resistance than single-phase TiZrHfTax counterparts.
State-of-the-art single-phase TiZrHfTax alloys typically have lower performance in one or more relevant mechanical properties than the proposed dual-phase alloy.
Coarse precipitates, excessive matrix softening, or nonuniform phase distributions can prevent the desired mechanical-property synergy.
The magnitude of the mechanical-property improvement will depend on precise control of composition and heat-treatment parameters.
